messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 19
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Unemployed
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 61

She is nineteen and newly married, living with her husband in a small basement apartment that still smells faintly of fresh paint and laundry soap. From the outside, her life looks as if it has just begun. She talks sometimes about wanting a job, maybe retail or childcare, something to help with bills and to get her out of the apartment during the day. But most mornings she wakes already exhausted, as if she has spent the night running.

The assault happens six months after the wedding. She has gone alone to a convenience store a few blocks away just after dark, wearing her husband’s oversized hoodie because the evening turns cold. On the walk back, a man she does not know follows her into the alley behind the building and attacks her. She remembers fragments with unnatural clarity: the scrape of concrete against her palm, the smell of beer on his breath, the way her mind seems to leave her body for a few seconds and hover somewhere above the scene. Other parts are gone entirely. When she tries to tell the story later, she gets stuck between sharp images and blank spaces.

In the first days afterward, she moves as if underwater. She startles when doors close. She cannot bear the hoodie and stuffs it into the back of the closet, then feels ashamed for hiding it because it belongs to her husband and has done nothing wrong. Family members urge her to rest, to stay close to home, to focus on healing. She nods and says little. At night she lies rigid beside her husband, waiting for sleep and dreading it. When she does drift off, she wakes with her heart pounding, convinced for a moment that someone is in the room. Sometimes she reaches out and grabs her husband’s arm so hard that he jerks awake.

As the weeks pass, the world becomes organized around danger. She checks the lock three or four times before bed, then once more after she gets back under the blanket. If her husband is late coming home, she calls him repeatedly and imagines stairwells, parking lots, strangers. She stops going to the convenience store, then stops walking anywhere alone. The alley behind the building feels like a trap; even seeing its entrance from the sidewalk makes her stomach turn. When friends invite her out for coffee, she says she is tired or not feeling well. It is easier to stay inside where she can control the light, the noise, the doors.

She had been looking for work before the assault, filling out applications online and talking about saving for a better apartment. Now even the idea of an interview makes her chest tighten. She imagines sitting across from a manager who asks ordinary questions while she tries not to scan every exit. Crowded buses feel unbearable. Men who stand too close in line make her skin prickle. She tells herself she is lazy, that other people go through worse and keep going, but the self-criticism only deepens her sense that something in her has been altered.

Her husband tries to be patient. He offers to walk her everywhere, to stay home more, to hold her when she cries. Sometimes she leans into him so completely that she feels like a child. Other times his touch startles her before she can think, and she pulls away, then apologizes over and over. Their marriage, still so new, becomes shaped by things neither of them expected: the lamp left on all night, the grocery trips timed for midmorning when the streets feel safer, the way she listens from the bathroom if he moves suddenly in another room.

She does not talk easily about the assault. When she tries, her throat closes and her eyes fix on a corner of the room. Certain sounds pull her back without warning—the heavy footstep of a stranger on stairs, a bottle clinking in a paper bag, laughter from men outside at night. In those moments she is no longer fully in the present. Her body goes cold and alert; she forgets what she was doing; she sees again a hand, a wall, the dark mouth of the alley. Afterward she feels embarrassed and angry at herself, especially when it happens over something small, like hearing someone behind her in the grocery aisle.

Now, months later, she spends most days indoors while her husband is at work. She keeps the television on for company but cannot follow what she watches. She sits by the window and monitors who comes in and out of the building. She wants the life she imagined at nineteen—work, friends, a home that feels safe, a marriage not crowded by fear. Instead she lives in a body that will not stop bracing for what already happened, and in a world that no longer feels ordinary.
